Framing novelty in crowdfunding: Which words win support, where, and at what stakes
abstract: Abstract Research Summary We examine how promotional language (“hype”) in reward‐based crowdfunding is associated with campaign success, and whether those associations vary across sector contexts and with campaign execution burden. Using dictionary‐based text measures from 635 U.S. Kickstarter campaigns across five sectors, we distinguish three novelty‐framing moves: capability/rigor language, excellence/status language, and attitude/affect language. We find no uniform association between aggregate hype and success. Instead, the observed associations vary systematically across rhetorical moves, sectors, and goal levels. Capability/rigor language is positively associated with success in Technology, attitude/affect language is positively associated with success in Entertainment, and excellence/status language is negatively associated with success in Design. Beyond these sector differences, the paper's clearest cross‐cutting pattern is that capability/rigor language becomes more positively associated with success as funding goals increase. Managerial Summary The value of “hype” on Kickstarter depends on what is said, what is being offered, and how ambitious the ask is. In our data, Technology campaigns are more positively associated with success when descriptions emphasize testing, technical specificity, and execution readiness, whereas Entertainment campaigns are more positively associated with attitude/affect language. In contrast, excellence/status claims are associated with lower success in Design. Across contexts, the clearest pattern is that feasibility‐oriented language becomes more positively associated with success as funding goals increase, suggesting that larger asks benefit more from cues of deliverability than from undifferentiated promotional intensity.

title: Academic entrepreneurs' material engagements in the creation of science‐based ventures
abstract: Abstract Research Summary This paper examines the creation of entrepreneurial opportunities under coupled technical and demand uncertainty within science‐based ventures (SBVs). Whereas opportunity creation theory emphasizes discursive processes, we build on practice theory and pragmatism to explore how SBV opportunities also emerge through entrepreneurs' evolving engagements with indeterminate material artifacts. Through a longitudinal multiple‐case study, we identify two patterns of material engagement: epistemic engagement, oriented toward knowledge creation, and pragmatic engagement, oriented toward practical use. We show how opportunity creation unfolds through interweaving cycles of epistemic and pragmatic engagement. By introducing material engagements as constitutive, we specify creation theory for SBVs and highlight the central role of materiality in shaping belief formation, opportunity objectification, stakeholder engagement, and the variation–selection–retention process. Managerial Summary This paper explores how entrepreneurs create science‐based ventures (SBVs) by engaging with evolving material artifacts, like sensors and prototypes. Based on a study of SBV initiatives supported by the European Commission's ATTRACT program, we identify a process in which entrepreneurs repeatedly alternate between epistemic engagement—focused on scientific understanding—and pragmatic engagement—focused on usability and implementation. This material engagement cycle plays a central role in venture development under coupled technical and demand uncertainty. We highlight tensions inherent in this process and the strategies through which they are accommodated, offering practical insights for entrepreneurs building ventures from frontier science and policymakers supporting science commercialization.

title: Visionary, engineer, and experimenter: Three forms of entrepreneurship in the quest for product–market fit
abstract: Abstract Research summary Entrepreneurship unfolds under uncertainty, which complicates entrepreneurs' efforts to align idea, action, and environment to reach product–market fit. To illuminate how entrepreneurs perform such alignment, we complement the theory‐based view and its focus on cognitive uncertainty with a discussion of behavioral uncertainty. We propose that entrepreneurs face four types of uncertainty: (1) uncertainty about the state of their environment (state uncertainty), (2) uncertainty about the interpretation of environmental cues (perception uncertainty), (3) uncertainty about the feasibility of turning an idea into a tangible product (execution uncertainty), and (4) uncertainty about the effect of their action in the environment (effect uncertainty). To mitigate these forms of uncertainty, entrepreneurs engage in idea–environment (entrepreneurs as visionaries), idea–action (entrepreneurs as engineers), and action–environment (entrepreneurs as experimenters) alignment. Each of these alignment strategies is associated with benefits and constraints in mitigating the uncertainty discussed. Our paper thus generates new insights into the nature of uncertainty and its effective mitigation in the quest for product–market fit, a critical precursor of success in entrepreneurship. Managerial summary Entrepreneurship succeeds when product and market are aligned. We map two sources of uncertainty that stand in the way of reaching product–market fit. Agentic uncertainty concerns the entrepreneur: interpreting signals (perception uncertainty) and making the idea work (execution uncertainty). Environmental uncertainty concerns the market: what state the market is in (state uncertainty) and how the market will react to products (effect uncertainty). Entrepreneurs can mitigate these uncertainties via three complementary strategies: (1) idea–environment alignment (“visionary” scanning the environment), (2) idea–action alignment (“engineering” to prove feasibility), and (3) action–environment alignment (“experimenter” testing to learn what sells). Each alignment strategy yields benefits and costs toward reaching product–market fit. In combination, they accelerate product–market fit—a critical driver of success in entrepreneurship.

title: It's a match! Similarity in personality traits in the business angel–founder dyad and follow‐on funding
abstract: Abstract Research summary We assess how personality alignment in investor–founder dyads is associated with the likelihood of follow‐on funding, a vital outcome for early‐stage ventures. Using machine learning to infer the Big Five personality traits from Twitter data for 9497 business angel–founder dyads, we find that similarity in conscientiousness and agreeableness is associated with a higher likelihood of follow‐on funding, while similarity in neuroticism is associated with a lower likelihood. We attribute these patterns to the trait‐specific benefits of supplementary (conscientiousness and agreeableness) and complementary (neuroticism) fit. Robustness checks and additional analyses support and nuance the conclusion that personality fit matters for venture outcomes, highlighting the strategic role of personality fit in the investor–founder relationship. Managerial summary We show that personality similarity between business angels and founders is associated with whether a venture secures follow‐on funding. Similarity in conscientiousness (being organized and reliable) and agreeableness (being cooperative and trusting) is linked to a higher likelihood of securing follow‐on funding, while similarity in neuroticism (emotional instability) is linked to a lower likelihood. We interpret these patterns as collaboration dynamics: similarity can help through supplementary fit (e.g., shared work style and cooperation), but differences can help through complementary fit (e.g., one partner's emotional stability offsets the other's emotional instability). Practically, founders and business angels should develop self‐awareness and consider personality fit alongside other characteristics when forming partnerships. Policymakers and incubators can support better matches and strengthen collaboration by promoting awareness of interpersonal dynamics.

title: Two hearts that beat as one: Signals, narratives, and financing (less) novel ventures via equity crowdfunding
abstract: Abstract Research Summary Financial resource acquisition is crucial for ventures but hindered by uncertainty. While signaling mitigates this uncertainty, its effectiveness hinges on venture novelty and the narratives used to clarify embedded information. Adopting a configurational lens, we examine the interplay among novelty, signals, and narratives in equity crowdfunding (ECF). Applying qualitative comparative analysis (QCA) to 98 ventures on a UK ECF platform, we reveal multiple equifinal pathways to fundraising success and demonstrate that novelty acts as a critical contingency factor: novel and less‐novel ventures require distinct configurations of signals and narratives, and narratives that clarify signals play a crucial role for novel ventures. Our findings extend research on signaling theory, entrepreneurial narratives, and entrepreneurial finance with a nuanced understanding of the interdependence among novelty, signals, and narratives. Managerial Summary Novel and less‐novel ventures face distinct challenges in convincing investors, and we show that there is no “one‐size‐fits‐all” strategy in fundraising. Our study demonstrates how entrepreneurs can convince investors using signals and/or narratives that align with the novelty of their ventures. For novel ventures, specific and coherent narratives are particularly helpful in clarifying signals that contain complex information. Conversely, less‐novel ventures that refine existing offerings may improve fundraising performance by simply emphasizing signals that demonstrate clear product‐market fit. We therefore suggest that entrepreneurs should view signals and narratives as complementary tools and tailor their fundraising strategies to match their ventures' novelty and achieve fundraising success.

title: Correction to “Are non‐economic goals and financial performance friends or foes in hybrid ventures? A duality perspective on academic spin‐offs”
Learning to innovate: How and when firms transform intellectual capital into exploratory and exploitative innovation
abstract: Abstract Research Summary Corporate entrepreneurship (CE) requires firms to pursue both exploratory and exploitative innovation, yet limited research explains how intellectual capital (IC) is translated into these distinct outcomes. We develop a contingency model that specifies how and when IC drives exploration and exploitation. We theorize that a firm's capacity for learning and transformation (CLT) functions as a firm‐level learning and transformation capability through which IC can be translated into either exploratory or exploitative innovation. Knowledge breadth strengthens the indirect effect of IC on exploratory innovation via CLT, whereas knowledge depth amplifies the indirect effect on exploitative innovation. We test the model in two complementary field studies. Study 1 employs a time‐lagged design with objective archival data, and Study 2 replicates the findings using survey data. Results consistently support the proposed theoretical model. Managerial Summary Firms operating in fast‐changing and uncertain environments often struggle to balance developing new products with improving existing ones. Our study shows that simply having strong knowledge resources is not enough. What matters is how effectively firms learn from and use that knowledge. We find that firms perform better when they build strong learning capabilities that help them adapt, recombine, and apply knowledge over time. Importantly, the type of knowledge a firm holds shapes this process: broad knowledge supports new product development, while deep, specialized knowledge strengthens improvements to existing products. For managers, this means focusing not only on acquiring knowledge but also on building systems and practices that continuously translate knowledge into action and innovation.

title: Dancing to multiple tunes: Establishing legitimacy with first‐time and repeat backers in crowdfunding campaigns
abstract: Abstract Research Summary Using 14,108 Kickstarter crowdfunding campaigns, we examine three strategies to gather support from first‐time versus repeat backers: narrative distinctiveness aligning with backers' expectations of novelty, endorsement from Kickstarter staff, and campaign leadership's reciprocity of funding other campaigns. Staff endorsement is more strongly associated with support from first‐time backers, while campaign leadership's reciprocity is associated primarily with repeat backers. Differences between first‐time and repeat backers are evident in evaluating narrative distinctiveness: narratives distinct from past campaigns correlate positively with repeat backers and greater funding but negatively with first‐time backers. Narratives distinct from live campaigns correlate positively with first‐time backers but are associated with lower funding amounts. Our findings conceptualize differences between first‐time and repeat backers that shape the associations between campaign legitimization strategies and backer support. Managerial Summary This work examines how Kickstarter campaigns should be designed to attract both new people and get support from existing community members. We test whether differences between these two target groups exist in evaluating commonly established “success factors” of campaigns: An endorsement from Kickstarter, the involvement of the campaign founder on the platform, and a campaign text highlighting the campaign's novel contributions. We find differences in all three between both groups and conclude with insights on how managers should design crowdfunding campaigns based on long‐term goals and objectives. We also offer some implications for crowdfunding platforms, such as Kickstarter, in supporting content creators in attracting new backers, which aids with overall platform growth.

title: Getting aggressive abroad through CEO and outside director stock options: An incentive‐based view of post‐entry internationalization pace of young entrepreneurial post‐IPO firms
abstract: Abstract Research Summary This study develops an incentive‐based view to examine the internationalization pace of young entrepreneurial firms after they have completed an IPO and expanded abroad for the first time. Using a sample of U.S. young entrepreneurial post‐IPO firms that internationalized from 2005 to 2020, we find that the pace of internationalization increases when CEOs are compensated with more stock options and that this relationship is weakened when the stock option compensation of independent outside directors increases. By showing that incentives of different agents shape how fast young entrepreneurial firms internationalize, this study extends international entrepreneurship research by relaxing the implicit assumption that young entrepreneurial post‐IPO firms that can internationalize fast will do so. Managerial Summary What determines the internationalization pace of young entrepreneurial firms after they have already completed an IPO and expanded abroad for the first time? Our research finds that the internationalization pace of these firms increases when the CEO is compensated with more stock options. Absent CEO stock options, stock option compensation of independent outside directors provides a substitute through monitoring and advocacy for faster internationalization. Our research highlights that young post‐IPO firms that can internationalize fast will not necessarily do so, stressing the distinction between the firm resources needed for a strategic action and top management motivation to pursue that action.

title: Toward a theory of Bayesian experimentation in early‐stage ventures
abstract: Abstract Research Summary The entrepreneurship literature has established the benefits of experimentation but has paid comparatively little attention to its costs. We develop a Bayesian model to illustrate the entrepreneurial choice between direct and experimental entry. We argue that performance depends on three mechanisms: information, adaptation, and appropriability. We show that experimental entry is not universally optimal and characterize the conditions under which each mechanism favors or undermines it. We further allow founders to hold biased prior beliefs, showing that greater bias increases the value of experimentation. Extending the baseline model to a multidimensional setting, we show that experimenting across different dimensions leads to a variety of counterintuitive insights. Our analysis produces a series of testable predictions and yields several implications for the broader entrepreneurship literature and practice. Managerial Summary Should every startup run experiments before launching? The lean startup movement says yes—but the answer depends on factors often overlooked by founders and investors. Experimentation creates value when the market is genuinely uncertain and founders' beliefs are far from what customers want. It can backfire when feedback is too noisy to interpret, when pivoting is prohibitively costly, or when releasing an early product may favor imitation. In settings where products have several significant features, which dimensions to experiment in matters as much as whether to experiment at all. Our findings offer guidance to entrepreneurs, investors, and policymakers designing the conditions that make experimentation feasible.

title: Hatching and fledging? A meta‐analysis of the performance effects of business incubators
abstract: Abstract Research Summary Business incubators are among the most widely implemented instruments to foster entrepreneurship. Yet empirical evidence on their effectiveness remains fragmented and often contradictory. Limited research systematically compares how different types of incubators influence multiple venture performance outcomes, including innovation, survival, growth, profitability, and employment. In this meta‐analysis of 39 empirical studies encompassing 55,219 firms, we synthesize the relationship between business incubation and different venture performance dimensions. Our results reveal a significant positive overall effect, moderated by the types of support mechanisms provided and the incubators' ownership identities. We find strong positive effects on innovation and a modest but statistically significant effect on growth, whereas effects on survival, profitability, and employment are weaker and, in part, statistically insignificant. Managerial Summary Policymakers regularly invest in incubators, yet uncertainty remains about which models deliver meaningful value to supported firms. Drawing on evidence from 39 studies covering more than 55,000 firms, this meta‐analysis shows that incubators can improve innovation and firm growth, while effects on survival, profitability, and job creation are limited or inconsistent. Incubator design and governance are central drivers of support effectiveness. Programs that emphasize bridging—that is, linking startups to investors, customers, and expert networks—generate stronger outcomes than models focused primarily on buffering, such as subsidized space or administrative support. Private and university incubators outperform public models, which often face bureaucratic constraints. These findings provide guidance on how managers and policymakers can align an incubator's support model and governance with the specific outcomes they seek to achieve.

title: Why theory matters for causal inference? Rethinking endogeneity in entrepreneurship research
abstract: Abstract Endogeneity in entrepreneurship research is often treated as a statistical complication addressable through advanced econometric tools. This commentary argues that such an approach overlooks a deeper issue: endogeneity is conceptual before it is statistical. Because entrepreneurial phenomena involve reciprocal relationships, evolving mechanisms, and context‐dependent processes, biased estimates frequently stem from underspecified constructs and unclear causal logic. I contend that theory, sufficiently precise to specify constructs, articulate mechanisms, and establish temporal ordering and boundary conditions, is the primary tool for reducing endogeneity in empirical estimation. Integrating theory with structural causal modeling and rigorous empirical design strengthens identification while enhancing explanatory value. I conclude with practical recommendations for scholars, emphasizing theory's central role in producing credible, cumulative knowledge in entrepreneurship research. Managerial Summary Entrepreneurs and managers often rely on data to understand what drives venture success, but data alone can be misleading if the underlying assumptions about cause and effect are unclear. This article explains why strong theory—clear ideas about how and why things work—is essential for drawing reliable conclusions from evidence. Endogeneity, a common problem in business research, occurs when factors influence each other in ways that make results appear stronger or weaker than they are. By using theory to map out mechanisms and likely confounding factors, leaders can make better decisions about which actions truly create value. The article also shows how tools like causal modeling can combine conceptual clarity with rigorous analysis, helping organizations design strategies that are both evidence‐based and trustworthy.

title: Temporal grammars of novelty: How carbon removal entrepreneurs frame new technologies
abstract: Abstract Research Summary This paper assesses the ways in which carbon dioxide removal ventures frame their work. Drawing on George Herbert Mead's philosophy of the present, it conceptualizes temporal grammars of novelty as a framing strategy that involves connecting two points in time, namely present and future, to elaborate novelty. Dictionary, dependency parsing, and large language model approaches trace the use of temporal grammars of novelty across the websites of carbon removal companies in the market, and connect this to venture sales volumes. Analyses show that ventures deploying newer technologies and using temporal grammars of novelty have higher sales. In contrast, explicitly causal language does not prove beneficial. This paper addresses a fundamental problem in conceptualizing novelty by arguing that it is referential without being causal, and shows this with reference to the framing strategies deployed by environmental entrepreneurs. Managerial Summary Carbon removal entrepreneurs must convince buyers that novel, often unproven technologies are credible. This paper shows that how they talk about time matters. Analyzing website language and sales across carbon removal ventures, it finds that firms using more speculative technologies sell more when they link present action to future possibility: what they are designing, building, or deploying now, and what this will make possible later, at scale. By contrast, causal language—detailed claims about why or how specific features will produce outcomes—is not helpful and is negatively associated with sales. When framing novelty, pairing present action with future promise is more credible than over‐specified causal certainty.

title: Co‐explorers of the imaginary: How fictional framing legitimates radical novelty by connecting entrepreneurial imagination to stakeholder possibilistic thinking
abstract: Abstract Research Summary The importance of entrepreneurial framing for legitimating novelty is well established, but the distinct challenges of legitimating radical novelty have received less attention. We articulate these challenges and propose fictional framing—the strategic and imaginative construction of a narrative world that blends the real and the imaginary using the practices of fictionalizing—as a means for addressing them. Drawing on literary theory, narratology, and the psychology of fiction, we theorize how fictional framing can engage stakeholders in co‐imagining through specific imaginative impacts. We further theorize how stakeholder co‐imagining fosters possibilistic thinking, changing their evaluative logic from focusing on likelihood and fit to what could be possible. Our framework extends the entrepreneurial framing toolkit by theorizing the distinct mechanisms for legitimating radical novelty through fictional framing. Managerial Summary When entrepreneurs pursue radically novel ventures, from space habitation to de‐extinction, conventional framing strategies that emphasize fit with existing knowledge and market categories are often ineffective. We propose that entrepreneurs can instead use fictional framing—the strategic and imaginative construction of a narrative world that blends the real and imaginary using fictionalizing practices. Unlike hype, which inflates expectations, fictional framing invites stakeholders to co‐imagine possibilities and evaluate radically novel projects based on their transformative potential rather than their probability of success. Leveraging the power of fiction to transport, support mental simulation, and prompt audiences to envision themselves acting within the imagined world, we propose how entrepreneurs can turn stakeholders into co‐explorers of the imaginary—active participants in co‐imagining and co‐creating consequential futures.

title: Mixed feelings, mixed outcomes? When emotionally ambivalent framing enhances idea appreciation
abstract: Abstract Research Summary Despite growing interest in how linguistic strategies shape audience responses to innovative ideas, prior evidence on the benefits of using emotional language remains mixed. Building on research on emotional ambivalence and social evaluation, we introduce the concept of emotionally ambivalent framing (i.e., the combination of positive and negative emotional language when presenting ideas) and investigate its effects on audience evaluation. Analyzing data from 3284 TED Talks, we find that emotionally ambivalent framing increases receptivity, but only for typical ideas. For atypical ideas, instead, such framing tends to undermine the audience's appreciation. However, we show that speakers' fame mitigates this effect, enabling emotionally ambivalent framing to serve as an effective communicative strategy for atypical ideas as well. These findings advance our understanding of the interplay between emotions and cognition in shaping the effectiveness of linguistic framing, contributing to research on entrepreneurship, ambivalence, and social evaluation. Managerial Summary It is still unclear whether and when using emotional language to frame ideas helps innovators and entrepreneurs overcome audience resistance. In this study, we find that combining both positive and negative emotional language when presenting an idea (a strategy we call emotionally ambivalent framing) improves audience receptivity to typical ideas. However, an emotionally ambivalent framing loses its effectiveness for atypical ideas. We also find that this effect depends on how well‐known entrepreneurs are: for famous ones, emotionally ambivalent framing becomes a powerful tool for increasing audience receptivity, particularly for atypical ideas. Overall, we show how innovators and entrepreneurs can strategically leverage emotional language and craft effective framing strategies that shape how audiences evaluate their ideas.

title: Novelty and its genealogy: The role of discarded prototypes as repositories of innovation
abstract: Abstract In markets where consumers seek both novelty and familiarity in products, entrepreneurs generate prototypes that embody novel ideas but are often filtered out before market release. We propose that these discarded prototypes constitute reservoirs of novel product content that can later be repackaged in more acceptable ways to decision makers and consumer audiences. To evaluate this argument, we analyze the genealogy of U.S. primetime television series from 1955 to 1995, tracing how novelty flows across both broadcast series and unsold pilots. The results show that, conditional on launch, series whose novelty derives more from unsold pilots than from prior series achieve greater market success. These findings support the argument that discarded products can serve as ‘hidden’ repositories of innovation, shaping future outcomes through recombination and reframing. We discuss implications for entrepreneurship research, emphasizing how creators need to position and frame novelty to gain gatekeeper support and how gatekeepers can avoid systematically undervaluing novel recombinations. MANAGERIAL SUMMARY This study examines how ideas abandoned during product development can become a source of competitive advantage. Our analysis shows that unsold television pilots contain more novel content than aired series, and using novel content from these pilots results in greater audience viewership. Broadly, this suggests that early‐stage concepts that do not advance can still inform effective product positioning. For managers and entrepreneurs, the opportunity lies in reusing novel features from these prior efforts and presenting them in ways that make their value recognizable to decision makers. This requires repositioning the idea and explaining why it is more compelling in the current context, how potential risks have been reduced, and what conditions make adoption timely.

title: Unleashing the value of a “scientific approach” to entrepreneurship: Building an empirical research agenda
abstract: Abstract Research Summary In this manuscript, we argue that the Entrepreneurs‐as‐Scientists (E‐a‐S) research program requires a fundamental shift from predominantly conceptual development toward an empirical agenda to achieve its normative goal: developing a scalable algorithm that improves entrepreneurial learning and value creation. The E‐a‐S approach prescribes that entrepreneurs learn by articulating causal theories, testing them, updating their beliefs, and revising their theories. We identify three risks of continued emphasis on conceptual development: overlooked complementarities, insufficient attention to boundary conditions, and potential overprescription based on limited evidence. We propose an empirical research agenda, as well as specific topics within it, to ground the E‐a‐S approach in systematic evidence, advancing a research program that is as rigorous in its methods as the entrepreneurial practices it seeks to improve. Managerial Summary This manuscript examines a growing approach that encourages entrepreneurs to think and act like scientists—by clearly articulating assumptions, testing them through experiments, updating beliefs, and refining their strategies. The goal is to develop a reliable, scalable method that improves how entrepreneurs learn and create value. However, current insights and ongoing research projects predominantly focus on conceptual work. We highlight three practical risks of such a focus: missing complementarities, overlooking when the learning method works best, and applying it too broadly without sufficient validation. We suggest that entrepreneurs use this approach flexibly since it was not designed to be a fixed formula. Ongoing research will clarify how to adapt it across contexts, helping entrepreneurs make more informed, disciplined, and effective strategic decisions.

title: Experimentation on a leash: How stakeholder influence shapes entrepreneurial experimentation across the venture lifecycle
abstract: Abstract Research Summary Prior studies have often conceptualized entrepreneurial experimentation as an activity over which founders exert a high amount of discretion in decision‐making. However, the locus of control over experimentation programs is dynamic, shifting with varying external stakeholder influence and venture growth. This paper proposes an integrative framework explaining how different stakeholder influence mechanisms function as frictions or enablers, shaping a venture's experimentation program. Resource provision mechanisms determine ventures' capacity for experimentation, while stakeholder strategic orientation and governance mechanisms shape the context within which ventures experiment, influencing how ventures deploy resources toward experiments. We further discuss how a venture's development stage shapes the relative value and impact of these stakeholder influences. Managerial Summary Experimentation and the Lean Startup approach are well‐established methods for navigating the inherent uncertainties of entrepreneurial ventures. While conventional wisdom often portrays founders as exercising substantial discretion over experimentation, this research demonstrates that a venture's experimentation program can be systematically shaped by external stakeholders. Rather than being solely founder‐driven, entrepreneurial experimentation is embedded in a broader stakeholder context that conditions what can be tested, how broadly, and how radically. Stakeholders shape ventures' experimentation by providing and controlling resources, influencing strategic directions, and structuring governance relationships. Strategic attention to which actors influence experimentation, how that influence is exercised, and how its relative importance shifts across venture development stages is important for fostering experimentation and improving venture performance.

title: Ignited or depressed? Entrepreneurs' status inconsistency and philanthropic giving
abstract: Abstract Research Summary Research has long emphasized entrepreneurs' status as a driver of philanthropy. Extending this literature, we examine how status inconsistency—misalignment among perceived economic, social, and political status—is associated with entrepreneurs' philanthropic contributions. We develop two theoretically grounded but competing interpretations: compensation , which suggests that entrepreneurs may increase giving to offset perceived status imbalance, and resentment , which suggests that perceived imbalance may dampen prosocial engagement. Using a national survey of Chinese private entrepreneurs supplemented with qualitative interviews, we find that while higher perceived status in individual dimensions is positively associated with philanthropy, inconsistency across these status dimensions is, on average, negatively associated with it. Moreover, entrepreneurs from farmer backgrounds, compared with those from upper‐class origins, exhibit patterns consistent with stronger compensatory giving. These findings underscore the nuanced implications of multidimensional perceived status for entrepreneurial philanthropy. Managerial Summary Entrepreneurs' philanthropic behavior depends not only on how high their perceived status is but also on how consistent it is across different domains. When entrepreneurs experience status inconsistency—for example, being economically successful but perceiving weaker social or political standing—this imbalance may be associated with either efforts to compensate through giving or feelings of resentment that suppress it. Overall, entrepreneurs with unbalanced perceived status tend to give less, yet those from lower‐class backgrounds are more inclined to donate in ways consistent with status‐balancing motives. Our study highlights how the interplay of economic, social, and political status perceptions relates to entrepreneurial philanthropy.

title: When stakeholders are imposed: Non‐chosen stakeholder orientation and venture performance
abstract: Abstract Research Summary Extending stakeholder theory into the entrepreneurship context, we examine the performance implications of externally imposed stakeholder orientation, which we conceptualize as non‐chosen stakeholder orientation. Given the resource constraints, short time horizons, and high levels of uncertainty that characterize ventures, we argue that increased non‐chosen stakeholder orientation can hinder venture performance. Analyzing 3981 U.S. ventures founded between 1980 and 1995, our staggered difference‐in‐differences analysis shows that constituency statute enactment, which exogenously increases orientation toward non‐chosen stakeholders, is negatively associated with ventures' successful exits and external funding. Consistent with our theory, this effect is stronger for ventures with a majority of internal board members, as these ventures are likely to maintain a narrow set of chosen stakeholders. Our theory and findings contribute to the entrepreneurship and stakeholder management literatures by jointly considering the source of stakeholder orientation—whether voluntarily chosen or externally imposed—and the organizational context in which firms operate. Managerial Summary This study examines how engaging with “non‐chosen” stakeholders—those imposed on ventures through legal or regulatory frameworks—affects entrepreneurial outcomes. Using data from 3981 U.S. ventures founded between 1980 and 1995, we leverage the enactment of constituency statutes as an exogenous shock to non‐chosen stakeholder orientation. Our results show that greater focus on these stakeholders reduces the likelihood of successful exits, such as IPOs or acquisitions, and lowers the cumulative external funding ventures receive. This effect may arise because non‐chosen stakeholders often require time, attention, and resources, diverting focus from growth opportunities and performance goals. These findings highlight that legally imposed engagement with stakeholders can constrain entrepreneurial growth and performance.

title: Decomposing venture evaluation: Learning about belief formation
abstract: Abstract Research Summary Evaluating early‐stage ventures is difficult because observable signals of future quality are weak and noisy. How closely are evaluators' assessments related to venture quality, and do their subjective judgments add to the information already available about a venture? Using more than 1600 screening decisions from a venture incubator, we examine how judges use application information to evaluate ventures by rating them on a set of 14 criteria and providing an overall recommendation. Judges' beliefs as recorded in the grades of the criteria explain their recommendations well, but they are only weakly associated with venture quality. We document some systematic miscalibration in how criteria are weighted, though the miscalibrations largely even out when examining the correlation between recommendations and quality. Within the models we estimate, beliefs and recommendations predict venture quality no better than ventures' observable attributes. Experienced judges are more selective but identify high‐quality ventures only slightly better than novice ones. Managerial Summary Accelerators and incubators rely on expert judges to screen early‐stage ventures, but how much does this expertise add? Using more than 1600 screening decisions at a venture incubator, we assess how well judges identify high‐quality ventures and where their judgment falls short. We find that judges' recommendations are only modestly accurate. Judges form a recommendation from venture information by first rating a set of 14 criteria, but the beliefs formed are themselves only weakly tied to venture quality. Judges also misweight the evidence: several characteristics that matter most for quality carry little weight in their recommendation, while others sway decisions despite mattering little. Experience helps at the margin; seasoned judges are more selective and better at filtering out weak ventures, but they don't spot winners better than novices. A simple model using only the objective data that ventures report in their applications predicts quality as well as the judges do.

title: Women own differently: How women's decision‐making authority shapes owner teams' strategic choices in private firms
abstract: Abstract Research Summary The literature on the strategic role of ownership in creating firm value suggests that owners' ultimate decision‐making authority allows them to align their firms' strategic orientations with their idiosyncratic judgment. By integrating the strategic ownership literature with social role theory, we theorize how women owners' gender‐based judgment influences owner teams' strategic choices depending on the level of ownership (i.e., decision‐making authority) collectively held by women owners. Our empirical evidence, based on 42,667 European firms, suggests that greater ownership among women is associated with less risky strategic choices and a stronger social value‐creation orientation among owner teams. These relationships are partly contingent on whether or not women hold a block majority. Our findings contribute to the strategic ownership literature and advance research on women's entrepreneurship. Managerial Summary In this study, based on 42,667 European private firms led by owner teams, we investigate how women's ownership affects owner teams' strategic choices. Consistent with established behavioral differences between men and women, we find that greater decision‐making authority held by women owners is associated with less risky strategic choices and a stronger social value‐creation orientation among owner teams. These associations, to varying extents, are contingent on whether or not women on the team collectively hold a block majority. Our findings help owner teams reflect on how the gender composition of their teams and the distribution of decision‐making authority among owners jointly shape strategic choices. We also provide investors with new insights into how different ownership structures ultimately influence firms' broader strategic orientations.

title: Caught in the framing: How consumer reactivity links typicality and market appeal for creative products
abstract: Abstract Research Summary While consumers' perceptions of creative products' framing typicality are guided by existing category structures, research on social evaluation emphasizes consumers' active role in shaping and redefining these structures. To tackle consumers being caught in the framing, we propose consumer reactivity as a mediator between framing typicality and market appeal, defined as consumers' extension and modification of categorical guidance in social evaluations. Specifically, we suggest that creative products with less typical framings elicit greater consumer reactivity, which in turn enhances their market appeal. Empirical analyses of a unique dataset of games on Steam using BERT‐based measures, topic modeling, and psycholinguistic analysis (LIWC) lend support to our theoretical arguments. Our work contributes to creative market studies and the category literature. Managerial Summary Consumers typically rely on category cues, so products that fit expectations often seem more appealing. However, they also actively engage with products, exploring features that don't fit categorical expectations. We show that consumer reactivity explains this dynamic: creative products with less typical framings generate stronger engagement, which in turn boosts market appeal. Our analyses of a unique Steam game dataset using BERT‐based measures, topic modeling, and psycholinguistic analysis (LIWC) support this pattern. For practitioners, the key insight is to acknowledge the potential of seemingly less‐fit products. By thoughtfully monitoring consumer interests and initiatives and cultivating their engagement, creative producers can enhance the market performance of creative products.

title: Balancing coherence and resonance through linguistic framing: A longitudinal study of German biotechnology ventures' responses to the Covid‐19 pandemic
abstract: Abstract Research Summary Research suggests that ventures benefit from framing to gain audience support, yet how they utilize framing when exogenous shocks redirect attention remains unclear. Drawing on a longitudinal multiple‐case study of six biotechnology ventures following the COVID‐19 pandemic, we show how ventures balance coherence and resonance through framing pathways. Persevering ventures, committed to pre‐shock opportunities, maintained a “Blockbuster” framing, highlighting business viability to engage commercial investors. Flexible ventures, in contrast, adopted an “Emergency” framing, signaling responsiveness to societal threats to attract public investors, before transitioning to a “Preparedness” framing, emphasizing long‐term potential. Across both pathways, ventures anchored framings in a scientific perspective, signaling expertise and rigor. We theorize how ventures balance coherence and resonance through an anchoring frame that provides continuity and complementing frames that enable adaptation to shifting audience expectations. Managerial Summary Our study of six biotechnology ventures shows how high‐technology entrepreneurs communicate with investors during industry shocks, such as pandemics. We identify two distinct pathways. Ventures that pivot toward shock‐related opportunities benefit from adopting an “Emergency” framing, positioning themselves as addressing urgent societal threats to attract public investors. To sustain investor support over time, they subsequently shift to a “Preparedness” framing, highlighting their solutions' long‐term potential. Conversely, ventures that maintain their original strategies gain traction by consistently employing a “Blockbuster” framing, emphasizing their business case to attract commercial investors. Across both pathways, ventures reinforce credibility by anchoring their framings in scientific expertise, rigor, and the ability to address unmet medical needs. Pivoting ventures also leverage new applications to identify and capitalize on additional shock‐related opportunities.

title: Logical reframing: A theory‐based view of entrepreneurial persuasion
abstract: Abstract Research Summary Prior literature that addresses how entrepreneurs systematically deal with Knightian uncertainty has primarily focused on individual entrepreneurs but has largely neglected that, to be successful, entrepreneurs must also persuade others of their view of the future. Uncertainty implies that others may initially have different and potentially conflicting framings of the future. In this article we offer a belief revision framework for persuasion under uncertainty based on the idea of logical reframing: using and communicating theories and what‐if beliefs that allow recipients to draw logical conclusions in line with the sender's view. Our propositions identify the trade‐offs the receiver has to make between contradictory explanations in her mind so she can be persuaded. The central insight from our framework concerns the role of filters, which are sets of beliefs that create resistance against an argument. Overall, our article contributes by taking the theory‐based view of entrepreneurship to a multi‐agent setting. We also continue the formalization of the theory‐based view, introducing ranking theory, which can be used to model how agents revise their beliefs, to the management literature. Managerial Summary Entrepreneurs often need stakeholders to accept not only a proposed action but also a shared account of why that action can succeed under uncertainty. We develop a framework of logical reframing in which entrepreneurs use arguments to connect stakeholders’ existing beliefs to a desired conclusion. Persuasion requires a complete logical route to that conclusion, a theory whose weakest premise is sufficiently strong and can overcome any additional contradictions activated by the argument. We show that what‐if beliefs can prepare stakeholders to accept an argument but they can also generate resistance by connecting the argument to conflicting prior beliefs. Our framework helps entrepreneurs identify which assumptions require strengthening, which objections must be addressed, and when an alternative route to persuasion may be more effective.

title: Re‐thinking academic entrepreneurship: Micro, meso, and macro perspectives
abstract: Abstract Research Summary We summarize and synthesize the papers contained in the special issue and use these studies to illustrate key micro, meso, and macro dimensions of academic entrepreneurship, where micro focuses on the scientist, meso is concerned with the university ecosystem, and macro refers to the broader entrepreneurial ecosystem. A key finding from our special issue is that routines, pivots, and intellectual property, which determine venture viability, emerge from granular individual action, including identity formation and evolution. We also find that macro instruments such as public funding/grants and institutional governance appear to steer resources toward viable science‐based ventures. Our essay concludes by presenting numerous additional micro, meso, and macro research questions to motivate future research on the managerial and public policy implications of academic entrepreneurship. Managerial Summary There are several key managerial implications of our essay and this special issue. “Managers” and those who supervise academic entrepreneurs need to develop and support their scientists entrepreneurial identity formation and evolution. Managers also need to enhance incentives for academic entrepreneurship and foster a culture within their academic departments, schools, and colleges that support these activities. Policymakers need to design entrepreneurial training for scientists with both “micro” and “macro” issues in mind.

title: Startup multihoming in enterprise software ecosystems: The role of skill breadth and organizational learning
abstract: Abstract Research Summary We investigate startup decisions to multihome to another platform. We develop a theory that shows startup engagement with the initial platform leads first to exploratory learning and later a shift toward exploitation, leading to an inverted U‐shape relationship between duration of platform partnership and the likelihood of multihoming. This tradeoff is shaped by the breadth of the startup's skill base. Startups with a broader set of skills initially face slower learning, but over time skill breadth provides greater adaptability that better positions them for multihoming. We test our theory using a novel dataset on SAP partners' multihoming decisions, examining the implications of Oracle acquisitions that increased the expected benefits of multihoming. Our empirical findings are consistent with our hypotheses. Managerial Summary The growth phase forms an important part of any startup's evolution, particularly when engaging with digital platform ecosystems, where expansion often depends on the ability to multihome. Startups' accumulated experience with a platform shapes how they respond when opportunities to expand to another platform arise. Startups with moderate levels of prior platform experience are most likely to expand, while longer relationships can create dependencies that reduce flexibility. Importantly, the breadth of a startup's skill base changes this trajectory. Startups with diverse skills are better able to avoid lock‐in and remain flexible, even after long partnerships. Evidence from the enterprise software ecosystem shows managers should see platform partnerships as both opportunity and risk, investing in broad skill sets to balance deep collaboration with the ability to grow across platforms.

title: How ventures maintain stakeholder support amidst operational legitimacy threats
abstract: Abstract Research Summary We explore how ventures mitigate operational legitimacy threats— threats that originate within the venture and challenge claims relating to the venture's ability to deliver on its promised value proposition . Through an inductive study of four ventures working to deliver their promised products following successful crowdfunding campaigns, we reveal a process of three rhetorical practices that ventures can use to maintain stakeholder support: humanizing the venture , normalizing setbacks and resolutions , and revising pragmatic claims . The first two practices contribute to the formation of dispositional legitimacy buffers that allow the third practice to be effective in mitigating fallout from exposed operational legitimacy threats. We conclude by offering contributions to the cultural entrepreneurship literature and to research on venture–stakeholder communication. Managerial Summary Entrepreneurs must often determine whether to disclose operational issues to stakeholders. On one hand, entrepreneurs may resolve these operational issues without stakeholders ever knowing of their occurrence. On the other hand, such issues could balloon to negatively impact whether a venture can deliver its promised offering. We identify three rhetorical practices, two of which entrepreneurs can utilize before an operational issue even occurs, to generate favorable judgments with stakeholders and increase the likelihood that their ventures will be able to maintain support if an operational issue becomes exposed.

title: Paid‐free differentiation in freemium: Understanding the balance between discovery and cannibalization and its implications for paid product sales
abstract: Abstract Research Summary Entrepreneurs in digital markets often introduce free versions of their paid products to boost their visibility. This freemium strategy involves a trade‐off between discovery and cannibalization. We study how feature‐based differentiation between the paid product and its free version shapes this trade‐off and its consequences for paid product sales. We theorize that the relationship between paid‐free differentiation and paid product sales is inverted U‐shaped, because moderate levels of paid‐differentiation significantly reduce cannibalization costs while discovery benefits remain largely intact. We further argue that paid‐free differentiation is more salient when the value of the free version is enhanced through network effects, but less so if the free version contains value‐eroding, third‐party advertising. We analyze paid apps from the iOS App Store utilizing the freemium strategy. Managerial Summary Freemium strategies by which entrepreneurs introduce a free product version to boost the discoverability of their paid product have become enormously popular in digital markets. But aside from providing discovery benefits, the free version also cannibalizes the paid product's sales. We investigate whether this trade‐off can be resolved through value‐adding, feature‐based differentiation between the paid product and the free version. Analyzing paid apps from the iOS App Store utilizing the freemium strategy, we find that there is a point of optimal paid‐free differentiation that favors substantial, though not maximal, differentiation. Paid‐free differentiation is especially important when the free version provides more value to consumers by means of network effects. Paid‐free differentiation is less important when the free version contains third‐party advertisements that erode its value.

title: Artificial intelligence and venture capital: Revisiting sourcing, selection, and nurturing activities
abstract: Abstract Research Summary Venture capital (VC) is an information‐intensive form of entrepreneurial finance conducted under extreme uncertainty. Investors must originate promising opportunities, select ventures with sparse and strategically disclosed information, and monitor and support firms after investment. Prior research documents both formal mechanisms (e.g., staged financing, syndication) and informal mechanisms built on referrals, reputation, and constant interaction. Geographic and social proximity enable these mechanisms by lowering the cost of obtaining contextual information and coordinating action. We develop a mechanism‐based account of how data and Artificial Intelligence (AI) reconfigure this established model. Our framework yields propositions on geographic dispersion in sourcing, portfolio selection, and the distinct effects of AI on monitoring versus value‐added support. It also identifies boundary conditions associated with institutional setting and heterogeneous AI adoption. Managerial Summary For venture capital firms, AI is not a single tool and adoption is not a binary choice. A fund may use data systems to identify founders, machine‐learning models to organize deal flow, generative AI to summarize diligence materials, or analytics to monitor portfolio companies. Each application changes a different part of the VC process. In sourcing, AI can widen the funnel beyond warm introductions and local ecosystems, especially in sectors such as software and e‐commerce where hiring, product, and customer signals are visible. In selection, AI can make diligence faster and more consistent, but models trained on past investments may favor ventures that resemble previously funded companies and may miss novel opportunities for which historical analogues are weak. In post‐investment activity, continuous operational data can partly replace physical presence for monitoring, while value‐add support such as customer introductions, recruiting, strategy advice, and founder coaching remain relationship‐intensive. The practical implication is a task‐level approach: automate codifiable search and processing, retain independent human judgment where uncertainty is fundamental, and use AI to strengthen rather than erode trusted investor–founder relationships. Funds also face organizational choices about building proprietary infrastructure, buying external tools, or combining the two. The appropriate configuration depends on data access, strategy, scale, and the activity in which the fund seeks advantage.

title: New wine, old bottles? Effective strategies of new GenAI firms
abstract: Abstract Research Summary Blending insights from GenAI, strategic reasoning, and empirical grounding in five illustrative ventures, we contribute a theoretical framework for effective strategies of new GenAI firms. They face bifurcated uncertainty (i.e., high uncertainty of a nascent market, moderate uncertainty of a somewhat predictable technology trajectory) such that two complementary strategic logics —Process Perspective (PP) and Resource‐based View (RBV)—are relevant. Second, we identify process‐based (i.e., well‐designed business model and product innovation process) and resource‐based (i.e., superior data, efficient orchestration, complementary resources) advantages. Some relate to GenAI, some generalize. Third, we address what is unique about GenAI entrepreneurship, including strategic implications of GenAI, technology strategy when there is upstream technical dominance and many downstream firms, and a cross‐technology comparison with technologies like software and predictive AI. Managerial Summary The rapid trajectory of GenAI is stunning. Yet many new GenAI firms are simply thin wrappers around well‐known LLMs. Drawing on five illustrative ventures, we contribute a framework for effective strategies for new GenAI firms. These firms face bifurcated uncertainty (i.e., high uncertainty of a nascent market, moderate uncertainty of a somewhat predictable technology trajectory). This calls for creating advantage by navigating high uncertainty markets to accomplish key strategic tasks and relying on foresight to build strategically valuable resources. Specifically, we identify process‐based (well‐designed business model and product innovation process) and resource‐based (i.e., superior data, efficient orchestration, complementary resources) advantages. We also address what is unique about GenAI entrepreneurship, including strategic implications of GenAI and a cross‐technology comparison with technologies like software, predictive AI, and quantum.

title: Value creation and capture in artificial intelligence‐enabled ecosystems
abstract: Abstract Research Summary We develop an ecosystem perspective on AI‐enabled value creation, grounded in AI's characteristics as a general‐purpose technology. We consider that AI can support multiple value propositions realized through distinct but interconnected ecosystems. Within this structure, AI innovators face choices concerning which value propositions to support, whether to pursue them through general‐purpose or specialized offers, and whether to make those offers open or closed. Users, in turn, are strategic actors facing choices among alternative ecosystem configurations of focal offers and complements through which the same value proposition might be realized. These choices by innovators and users may alter ecosystem roles and competitive relationships over time. We conclude by outlining research opportunities for strategy and innovation scholars examining how firms create and capture value in AI‐enabled ecosystems. Managerial Summary Value creation with AI depends not only on the technology's capability but on the actors whose combined contributions deliver a value proposition. AI supports many value propositions, each through its own ecosystem, with some elements shared across them. AI innovators choose which value propositions to serve, whether to do so through general‐purpose or specialized offers, and whether to make their offers open or proprietary. User firms choose among alternative configurations of offers and complements through which the same value proposition can be realized. These choices may shift the competitive relationships between actors within an ecosystem over time. This perspective surfaces questions of relevance for scholars and practitioners regarding value creation and capture with AI.

title: Whither business model innovation strategy in the age of AI ?
abstract: Abstract Research Summary We argue that business models are transformed into auto‐adaptive systems through embedded AI inference and learning activities. The competitive advantage of focal firms may increasingly depend on how effectively their activity systems learn relative to competing business models, with learning serving as a meta value driver. Such learning‐based advantages may be difficult to replicate when they are costly to create, path dependent, anchored in distinctive accumulated data, and rely on tightly coupled recursive feedback loops among business model activities. Entrepreneurs and corporate leaders thus become architects and curators of evolving learning systems and innovators of novel business models that are critical to their firm's value creation and sustainable performance. Managerial Summary The competitive advantage of focal firms increasingly depends on new AI learning and inference activities, which serve as meta‐value drivers in business models that learn faster, more broadly, and more reliably than competing business models. These dynamic learning‐based advantages are difficult to replicate because they are costly, path dependent, anchored in specific accumulated data, and rely on tightly coupled recursive feedback loops among business model activities. In this paper we argue that entrepreneurs and corporate leaders need to become architects and curators of evolving, auto‐adaptive learning systems and innovators of novel business models that are critical to their firm's value creation and sustainable performance.

title: Theorizing future phenomena: Metaverse, wearables, and humanoids
abstract: Abstract Research Summary We propose that entrepreneurship and strategy research can develop theory about phenomena of the future rather than only explain those of the past. Research has potential for practical relevance when researchers make claims towards applications to decisions practitioners have yet to make. Theory grounded in a world that may differ from the observed world can be built through a process of extrapolation from technological trends, a practice utilized by entrepreneurs and science fiction authors alike. Assuming advances in artificial intelligence, we apply this process to three emerging phenomena: governing scarcity in metaverse virtual worlds, redesigning organizations around pervasive monitoring via wearable devices, and allocating the intellectual property rights of humanoid robots. We argue that embracing theory that speaks to the future can enhance the practical and educational relevance of management research. Managerial Summary Assuming artificial intelligence continues to improve, we highlight three impending phenomena poised to transform conventional approaches to entrepreneurship and strategy. First, in metaverse virtual worlds, managers must manage resources governed by artificial scarcity. Second, with wearable devices allowing continuous monitoring, managers must consider alternative structures for vertical hierarchy and horizontal collaboration. Third, deployment of humanoid robots will complicate intellectual property rights and asset ownership. We propose that scholarship towards developing theoretical frameworks addressing these and other phenomena of the future will be relevant to both managers and students.

title: Entrepreneurial theorizing with generative artificial intelligence
abstract: Abstract Research Summary Whether large language model (LLM) assistance changes how entrepreneurs construct theories remains unclear. On the one hand, LLMs may help entrepreneurs build more developed causal structures and surface diverse information that supports the formulation of distinctive theories. On the other hand, LLMs may steer causal structures toward conventional forms and discourage the counterintuitive reasoning needed to develop distinctive theories. In a within‐subject experiment with 199 participants theorizing both with and without LLM assistance, we find no significant average treatment effect on either structural or content properties. However, this null average effect masks a redistribution effect, where LLM assistance supplemented theorizing when unaided theories were less developed or distinctive but displaced participants' own theorizing when their theories were already more developed or distinctive. Managerial Summary Large language models (LLMs) can help entrepreneurs develop business ideas by surfacing knowledge across domains and sharpening causal logic. At the same time, LLMs may also push reasoning toward conventional patterns and away from the counterintuitive ideas that are a source of breakthrough opportunities. In a study of 199 participants theorizing with and without LLM assistance, we find that LLMs supported the development of causal structure and content distinctiveness when unaided theories were less developed or distinctive, whereas they had the opposite effect when those theories were already more developed or distinctive. This suggests that while LLMs can scaffold entrepreneurs still developing their theories, greater caution is warranted for those whose theories are already more developed or distinctive, as assistance may diminish those properties.
